title: Mirador de Gràcia / Miriam Castells
text:
Mirador de Gràcia / Miriam Castells

The Barcelona-based studio Miriam Castells unveils the interior design for Mirador de Gràcia, a 6,600 m² senior living community nestled on the slopes of the Collserola Natural Park. Positioned right on the border between nature and the city of Barcelona, the project transforms a complex shared-living facility into a space where the human experience takes center stage. The project is grounded in a single core conviction: a senior living residence can—and absolutely must—feel like home.

title: Living Archive / Office ParkScheerbarth
text:
Living Archive / Office ParkScheerbarth

For the first time, 3,400 square meters of previously unused basement beneath a former East Berlin power station opened to the public. For these spaces, Berlin studio Office ParkScheerbarth developed a concept with Tresor founder Dimitri Hegemann for the permanent Living Archive of techno culture he first announced in 2015. The exhibition "Dancefloors After 1989" put it to a full-scale test. For its five-week run, the studio secured the permit and designed the exhibition, using material the building itself supplied.

title: Catching Fog: How Architecture Collects Water from the Air
text:
Catching Fog: How Architecture Collects Water from the Air

Where rivers, reservoirs, and rainfall can no longer be relied upon consistently, water is increasingly being sought in the atmosphere. Fog, atmospheric humidity, and condensation each offer different ways of collecting it. When architecture begins to collect water from the air, surfaces, structures, and open spaces become part of the water system.

title: Harfa Rooftop Extension / matěj šebek architekti
text:
Harfa Rooftop Extension / matěj šebek architekti

How can an urban apartment building be developed without turning it into a developer's product? The revitalisation of an apartment building in Prague's Vysočany offers a different approach to rental housing in Prague.

title: Beijing 1733 ByteDance Commercial Project / XU Studio
text:
Beijing 1733 ByteDance Commercial Project / XU Studio

In highly rational and efficiently operated office parks, how can commercial spaces evolve beyond their role as functional amenities and become shared environments with a sense of life and warmth? The Beijing 1733 Public Space Renovation responds to this question through a strategy of lightweight intervention. Xu Studio revitalized the sunken commercial space and interior themed areas through the insertion of architectural elements, landscape integration, and the reshaping of commercial scenarios, redefining the role of commercial spaces within office campuses.Guided by open interfaces, natural elements, and diverse commercial programs, the design transforms the originally restrained architectural environment into a more vibrant and engaging public space.

title: Sangwich Club / east bureau
text:
Sangwich Club / east bureau

Sangwich Club is a 109.3-square-meter sandwich bar in central Almaty, designed by east bureau as a place that reveals itself gradually. Rather than building the interior around a single visual gesture, the project brings together the existing character of the space, the brand's visual language, and a series of custom-designed elements that echo one another throughout the interior.

title: Dumas Sea Face Masterplan / INI Design Studio
text:
Dumas Sea Face Masterplan / INI Design Studio

For decades, Surat's relationship with the Arabian Sea was shaped by a fragmented and underutilized shoreline. The Dumas Sea Face Masterplan reimagines this edge as a living coastal landscape, transforming a neglected waterfront into a resilient public realm where ecology, civic life, and urban identity converge. Located along the historic Dumas coastline, the project responds to the growing demand for high-quality public open space in one of India's fastest-growing cities. Despite its long-standing cultural and recreational significance, fragmented development, limited accessibility, and the absence of a cohesive vision have constrained the shoreline's potential. The masterplan addresses these challenges by stitching together disparate segments into a continuous waterfront experience that reconnects the city with the sea.

title: AA Apartments / Crearctive
text:
AA Apartments / Crearctive

The project addresses the change of use of commercial premises to transform them into four independent apartments. Taking advantage of the open-plan layout of the original space and its generous clear height of thirteen feet (four meters), the proposal resolves the distribution by designing the void and working in section. The strategy relies on a central spine that groups the service spaces, which optimizes the layout of the building systems, frees up the perimeter of the home, and allows for the articulation of an intermediate level that makes the most of the height of the space.

title: MAGMA House / SUITE

title: Colares Sintra House / Sabrab
text:
Colares Sintra House / Sabrab

Set within a pine forest of stone pines in Colares, overlooking the vineyards and the slopes of the Sintra Mountains, the house is the result of transforming an existing villa into a contemporary living space, open to the garden and the landscape.

title: Shanghai Grand Opera House / Snøhetta
text:
Shanghai Grand Opera House / Snøhetta

Set along the Huangpu River, the Shanghai Grand Opera House emerges as a new cultural landmark for one of the world's most dynamic cities. As an open cultural landscape, it brings together a world-class performing arts venue and an accessible public realm – inviting residents and visitors alike to engage with culture, architecture, and urban life. Rooted in Shanghai's spirit of openness, exchange, and innovation, the project broadens access to culture while creating a new platform for artistic expression and civic engagement.

title: Bunkers and Arks: Escaping the Future We Built Ourselves
text:
Bunkers and Arks: Escaping the Future We Built Ourselves

Inverting the conventional narrative, this story begins at the end. The day after the world's collapse. While almost the entire population struggles to survive flames and solar storms, a tiny fraction is greeted by a heavily armed guard at the entrance to the Survival Condo Project, a former missile silo in Kansas converted a few years ago into luxury apartments.

title: Prague Fire Rescue Service / Architektura
text:
Prague Fire Rescue Service / Architektura

The Prague Fire Rescue Service headquarters complex in Holešovice is conceived as civic infrastructure anchored by a strong urban presence at a highly exposed intersection. The project develops a long-term strategy for the Fire Rescue Service to consolidate its operational and administrative functions within a coherent campus, combining clarity of organisation with a distinctly public architectural expression.

title: HARMAY Changsha Guojin Street Store / STUDIO SPLASH
text:
HARMAY Changsha Guojin Street Store / STUDIO SPLASH

Located on Guojin Street at the core of Changsha's Wuyi Square commercial district, the project sits within an underground retail spine linking street-level entrances with subterranean transit hubs, marked by crisscrossing interior corridors. The HARMAY store occupies the B1 level, bridging the B2 double-height atrium with the north-south ground access routes at a major intersection of pedestrian circulation.

title: Ella House / Studio Memo
text:
Ella House / Studio Memo

Casa Ella is divided into two blocks around a central garden, connected by a fluid path of ramps that link the zones at every half-level up to a roof garden, gradually revealing the relationships between the home's interior and exterior. It features a sculptural volumetry that embraces, protects, and welcomes, while also enabling multiple connections with the outdoors. Among the design solutions adopted, the project prioritizes the residents' privacy while offering spaces filled with natural light.

title: Pavilion for Good Sleep / WHALE!

title: Central Library at Stevens Ranch  / Miller Hull Partnership + Steele Associates Architects
text:
Central Library at Stevens Ranch / Miller Hull Partnership + Steele Associates Architects

Deschutes County's New Central Library Reimagines What a Library Can Be Designed by Miller Hull and STEELE Associates, the 100,000-square-foot Stevens Ranch library brings together learning, creativity, coworking and community through a mass-timber design. Stevens Ranch, Oregon — A library means something different to everyone. For some, it's a place to do research. Others come to read in peace, to write, to code, to collaborate. The new Central Library at Stevens Ranch in Deschutes County, OR, designed by The Miller Hull Partnership and local architects STEELE Associates, acknowledges these different user groups and welcomes them all. At over 100,000 square feet, the three-story library accommodates the diverse experiences of modern life and learning.

title: Two Multi-Family Housing Units / Aplomb
text:

This project involves the construction of two social housing units for SOMCO, the historical social housing provider (bailleur HLM) for the City of Mulhouse, which is widely renowned for its architectural heritage and social commitment. From its very inception, the project brief has demonstrated a strong environmental and eco-responsible ambition.

title: Transforming Barcelona's Waterfront: A Story of Urban Renewal
text:
Transforming Barcelona's Waterfront: A Story of Urban Renewal

As one walks along the beachfront of Barcelona, the shoreline feels like it has always been there: sand, palm trees, a long promenade, restaurants, shops and modern hotels, when the reality is that it has not always been this way. Until the 1980s, Barcelona's seafront was a working barrier of railway lines, factories and informal housing, and wastewater ran straight into the Mediterranean. Starting in 1987, Barcelona has continuously created large promenades and passages between the city and the sea, creating an environment that today many might read as previously empty space, but is actually the result of decades of infrastructure and social complexity, along with a municipal effort to transform the city's territory and its relationship to the water. Following that transformation raises three questions that frame this article: who was displaced to open the waterfront, who governs it today, and who keeps it standing?

title: City Pride School / A Threshold
text:
City Pride School / A Threshold

This primary educational institution, known as City Pride School, is situated in the newly developed region of Ravet Pradhikaran, Pune, characterized by densely populated urban neighborhoods. The school occupies a compact, high-rise urban landscape where the scarcity of space and significant commercial value necessitated a six-story design, limiting the availability of horizontal open and communal areas. In response to this challenge, the architectural design embraces a "school within a school" philosophy, structuring the building in a manner that ensures the spatial scales are perceived as intimate, thereby enhancing the learning environment. This approach aims to cultivate a self-sufficient educational setting that promotes a sense of community and interconnectedness.

title: What Should Exterior Insulation Do Beyond Thermal Performance?
text:
What Should Exterior Insulation Do Beyond Thermal Performance?

The buildings and construction sector accounts for around 39% of global CO₂ emissions and nearly 50 per cent of global material extraction. Operational carbon emissions which are associated with the energy consumed to run the buildings also rose by 1% to 9.9 billion tonnes of CO₂ in 2024, even as building energy use intensity (EUI) has improved. These figures point to persistent gaps in the way buildings are designed, constructed and upgraded. One important area for closing those gaps is the building envelope insulation, which remains central to controlling energy demand, improving thermal resilience and reducing carbon emissions.

title: Lion Green Road by Mary Duggan Architects and RUFFARCHITECTS Wins RIBA Stirling Prize 2026
text:
Lion Green Road by Mary Duggan Architects and RUFFARCHITECTS Wins RIBA Stirling Prize 2026

The RIBA Stirling Prize 2026 has been awarded to Lion Green Road, a housing development in Coulsdon, South London, designed by Mary Duggan Architects with RUFFARCHITECTS for Croydon Council. Comprising 157 homes across five residential blocks, the project combines privately owned and socially rented housing on a former car park. Presented annually by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA), the Stirling Prize recognizes a building considered to make a significant contribution to the evolution of architecture and the built environment. The 2026 winner was announced at a ceremony at Old Billingsgate in London on October 15, marking the prize's 30th anniversary.

title: Design in the material you ship
text:
Design in the material you ship

Designers should understand code the way an architect understands stone: what it can do, not how to cut it. AI now does the cutting.

Early in The Fountainhead, Howard Roark is expelled from architecture school for refusing to design in borrowed styles. The Dean calls him in to explain himself, and Roark gives him a rule instead: “What can be done with one substance must never be done with another. No two materials are alike. No two sites on earth are alike. No two buildings have the same purpose. The purpose, the site, the material determine the shape.”

You don’t have to admire Roark to take the point. He is the architect in the book who spends his time on building sites, among the electricians and steelworkers, learning what the material will and won’t do. His classmates learn to draw facades.

Digital designers have a material too. It is code. For most of the last fifteen years, we have designed in pictures of it. The warning is older than that. John Allsopp asked the web to stop imitating print in 2000, Frank Chimero wrote about working with the web’s grain in 2015, and Jeremy Keith gave its materials a chapter of their own in Resilient Web Design.

The drawing is not the building

A design file is a drawing. It shows one state, at one width, in one language, with the data the designer typed in. The product is every other state.

The name is longer than the box. A short English label can double in length once it is translated. The photo fails to load. The list is empty. The request takes four seconds, or fails. Someone tabs through with a keyboard. The phone is 320 pixels wide. None of those is an edge case to the person it happens to, and none of them exists in the file until someone draws it by hand, which in practice means rarely.

When the file is the source of truth, each of those gaps gets decided by whoever writes the code, after the design is called done, and usually without a conversation. The file and the product drift apart, and the file keeps being presented in reviews as if it were the product.

What changed when the code became the source

When I built 131 variations of one button to study hover feedback, I built them in code. The surprise was what happened to the specification. In a design file, a jelly button is an adjective: tactile. In code, it is a handful of numbers. The pointer starts to count 36 pixels from the edge, the material has a stiffness, and it settles back in under a second. An engineer can build a number. Nobody can build an adjective.

I now work the same way on a product team. The prototype in code is what gets reviewed. The design file still exists, because people like to leave comments on a canvas, but it is regenerated from the code after each pass, never the other way round. Its job is to be a mirror.

Roark’s rule applies almost word for word. A responsive layout, a loading state and a focus ring belong to the browser. Drawing them in a canvas tool is doing with one substance what belongs to another.

You no longer have to write it

This is where the old version of the argument went wrong. For a decade, “designers should code” meant designers should learn to write HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Many tried, many quit, and they were right to resent it. It asked them to become a second, slower engineer. Brad Frost later drew a more useful line, between the front of the front end, which sits close to design, and the application logic behind it.

That argument is over, because AI writes the code. I describe the screen, its states and its numbers, and the model writes it. I correct it by looking at the result and saying what is wrong, the way an architect corrects a site, not by laying the bricks again myself.

Reading code is going the same way. It still helps, and I read diffs most days. But AI review tools read them too, and they are improving quickly. In one benchmark this year, the best reviewer caught 84 of 122 real bugs taken from production codebases such as Sentry and Grafana. The vendor that won ran the test, and two thirds is not all of them. So the claim is not that the machine has replaced the reviewer. It is that the designer no longer needs to be the reviewer.

Engineers reading this will object, and they have a point. In Stack Overflow’s 2025 developer survey, 66 percent named AI answers that are almost right, but not quite, as their top frustration, and 46 percent said they distrust its accuracy. Someone accountable for the system still has to read what goes into it. That person is the engineer who owns it. The designer has a different job.

Understanding is the part you can’t delegate

What Roark took from the building site was not the skill of riveting. It was knowing what steel will do, so that his drawings only asked for things the material could give.

That is the part AI can’t hold for you. It will write whatever you describe, including things the medium handles badly, and it will review the code against the code, not against what the person on the other end needed. Judging that takes someone who knows the material.

You judge the output by running it, not by reading it. Open it at 320 pixels. Paste the longest real name you can find. Set the network to slow. Put the mouse away and use the keyboard. None of those tests needs a line of syntax.

What to learn instead of syntax

  • How layout flows: what wraps, what stretches, what refuses to shrink.
  • Which states exist: empty, loading, partial, failed, offline.
  • The shape of the data, including what a field holds when it holds nothing.
  • What costs a trip to the server and what is free on the device.
  • What a screen reader actually announces on your screen.
  • How to run the product on your own machine, without help.
  • How to ask the AI to explain a change in plain words.

None of these requires writing code. All of them require spending time with it.

The material determines the shape

Roark’s rule ends where this argument does: the purpose, the site and the material determine the shape. Our material hasn’t changed. It is still code, and it still decides what a screen can be. What changed is that we no longer have to hold the chisel to learn what it can cut.

Design in the material you ship was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Human in the loop means making sure the human is not out of the loop
text:
Human in the loop means making sure the human is not out of the loop

Agents now act before we ask and reach past what we authorized. A person in the loop isn’t enough if nobody owns the outcome. Here’s what to consider when designing for it.

Agents used to wait for a prompt because everyone though that AI was only chat. Now they triage inboxes, update records, and send messages while we’re in another meeting. That’s the whole point of them, and it’s also where the trouble starts.

Because of this, most agent teams hit the same questions:

  • Should the agent act before the user asks?
  • When the agent does more than anyone authorized, who is liable for the call?

The standard answer is a confirm dialog. Add a human click, and the accountability problem is supposed to vanish. It moves instead, landing on whoever had the least information and the least power over the outcome.

None of this is new.

Eric Horvitz modeled when software should act alone in 1999. Sixteen years earlier, Lisanne Bainbridge warned in Ironies of Automation that automating most of a job leaves people holding its hardest part, the watching. What’s new is volume: Gartner predicts at least 15% of day-to-day work decisions will be made autonomously through agents by 2028.

I’m an apologist for artificial intelligence, and I’ll admit some things it isn’t good for.

The proactive question is mostly a decoy.

Initiative isn’t what hurts people; reach is. The better question is a reach test: what can the agent touch, and can a person put it back? The answer also settles liability.

Whoever sets an agent’s reach owns what it does there, and no confirm click should shift that to whoever clicked.

Stop Counting the Clicks

A confirm button records that a person was there; it says nothing about whether they read what they approved.

Kathleen Mosier and Linda Skitka named this automation bias in the 1990s, and it comes in two forms. Errors of commission follow the machine’s wrong suggestion, and errors of omission miss what the machine never flagged.

In Skitka’s 1998 NASA report, Automation: Decision Aid or Decision Maker?, people using an aid were 65% accurate when it was wrong, against 97% for people working without one. My Automation Bias entry at UX Guidelines calls omission the quieter failure, since nothing on the screen ever asks to be doubted.

Anthropic’s study of its own coding agent, Measuring AI agent autonomy in practice, found newer users ran full auto-approve in roughly 20% of sessions, rising past 40% for experienced users.

Those experienced users also interrupted more, in about 9% of turns against 5% for new ones.

Approval is a ritual. Interruption is a judgment, which is good.

Anthropic’s own conclusion is that forcing a human to approve every step adds friction without necessarily adding safety. The per-click version is a cousin of the security theater usually credited to Bruce Schneier: visible, reassuring, and blind to how far the agent can reach afterward. People still belong in the loop, just at the point where judgment holds up: watching a run they can stop, instead of pre-signing a list they can’t read.

Follow the Blame

Madeleine Clare Elish gave this its name in 2019. In Moral Crumple Zones, she showed how responsibility for a failure gets pinned on the human operator closest to the event, even when that person had little control over what the automated system did.

A car’s crumple zone protects the driver. The moral version protects the system, and the operator absorbs the impact.

This is the most telling example. In March 2018, an autonomous Uber test vehicle struck and killed Elaine Herzberg in Tempe, Arizona. A safety driver, Rafaela Vasquez, sat behind the wheel, in the loop by every definition the program used. Granted, Vasquez was watching television on her phone, but that further illustrates the point.

According to CNN’s report on the Uber test driver’s 2023 guilty plea, the federal safety board found Vasquez had looked away for more than a third of the trip, and that an inadequate safety culture at Uber contributed. Uber faced no criminal charges and the driver pleaded guilty to endangerment and got three years of supervised probation.

She paid the price for the human missing the loop.

Being in the loop, it turns out, mostly means being nearest the crash.

None of this excuses the distraction, but it shows where accountability flows when a system is built around a watcher it doesn’t support. The reviewer who clicked approve on step 41 of a 60-step run becomes the crumple zone, while the team that decided step 41 needed no stronger gate stays out of the story.

Price the Unasked Act

Eric Horvitz’s 1999 paper, Principles of Mixed-Initiative User Interfaces, still frames when software should act unasked. His rule is decision theory in plain clothes: act only when the expected value beats doing nothing.

His math leaves one variable implicit: whether the action can be undone. Drafting a reply and sending it carry the same chance of being right and very different costs of being wrong.

One way vs. two way doors: Proactivity should scale with reversibility, not with confidence.

An agent that prepares, drafts, flags, and stages work is extending the user’s reach inside a space they can still edit and undo. One that sends, deletes, pays, or commits is spending the user’s authority.

The accuracy an action needs should shape the interaction too. A probabilistic output is a prediction about what’s likely right, while a deterministic one is a certainty.

  • A summary can be a prediction and still be useful, because a reader applies judgment.
  • A decision that routes a claim, approves a payment, or marks a contract compliant has to be a deterministic certainty, coming out the same way every time on the same input. That pushes it toward explicit rules the model applies rather than invents.

Put both behind the same button and a prediction ends up dressed as a certainty. Dan Maccarone quotes a client’s rule in We’re gorging on borrowed trust and it’s going to cost us: “people conclude, machines don’t.”

All of this gets harder with ambient agents, which watch a queue or an inbox and act while nobody is looking.

  • A chatbot waits for a question, so a bad answer at least has a witness.
  • An ambient agent acts on its own schedule, often many times before anyone reads the log, so its mistakes compound quietly.

For ambient work, the reach test has to be answered entirely in advance, and the record becomes the first thing a person sees rather than the last.

Write the Mandate

An agent, in the legal sense, acts for a principal, and the principal answers for what the agent does within the authority it was given. A power of attorney writes that authority down: what it covers, for how long, revocable at will.

We need this because nobody signs one that just reads “use your judgment.”

Agency is the whole value of an agent, and control over that agency is the one thing a principal never hands across. A mandate is the reach test answered in advance, in writing.

In Moffatt v. Air Canada, the airline claimed it couldn’t be held liable for what its website chatbot told a customer about bereavement fares. A British Columbia tribunal called that “a remarkable submission” in 2024 and held the airline responsible for everything on its site. The company set the chatbot’s reach, so the company owned what it said. And that bot only spoke when a customer asked it something. Maccarone’s name for what Air Canada spent is borrowed trust, a brand’s reputation lent to output nobody checked.

A mandate lives in the permissions, not in the conversation.

The Replit incident in July 2025 shows what happens when the mandate exists only as a sentence. SaaStr founder Jason M. Lemkin froze his project and told the agent repeatedly not to change anything. It deleted the production database anyway, then wrongly reported that rollback was impossible.

The fix is decades old: least privilege, enforced by the system at the moment of action. An instruction the agent can ignore is only a preference, not a harness.

Check the Law

I’m not a lawyer, so read this as a designer’s map of where the rules point, not legal advice. Some decisions shouldn’t appear in any mandate at all. Article 22 of the GDPR gives people the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects.

Even its exceptions for contracts and consent still require a way to reach a human, state a view, and contest the outcome.

Newer laws push the same way:

  • EU Artificial Intelligence Act. Article 14 requires people overseeing high-risk systems to be able to override the output and stop the system, and it names automation bias outright. A Digital Omnibus in July 2026 pushed those duties for uses like employment to December 2027.
  • California CCPA. The state’s automated decisionmaking rules require notice and an opt-out for significant decisions from January 2027, unless people can appeal to a human who can overturn the decision.
  • Colorado ADMT Act. Colorado replaced its 2024 Artificial Intelligence Act in May 2026 with a law granting human review after an adverse decision, from January 2027 if rulemaking finishes.
  • New York City Local Law 144. Hiring tools have needed bias audits since 2023, yet a December 2025 state comptroller audit found 17 possible violations among 32 companies where the city found one.
The law can require a way back. We have to design one.

These laws cover the second half of the reach test, not the first. What an agent can touch is still a product decision, and my own list goes further.

  • Hire, fire, or discipline. Livelihood decisions need a named person who can explain the call, in court.
  • Deny care or benefits. Refusing a claim or a treatment deserves a human who weighed it.
  • Sign for the organization. Contracts and regulatory filings bind a company in ways no model can answer for.
  • Give advice under a professional’s name. Legal, medical, and financial advice carries a license, and licenses belong to people.
  • Move money past the point of recall. Irreversible payments above a set limit wait for a person.

Design for Ownership

Microsoft Research tested their Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction against 20 products in 2019. Two describe half the job:

  • Scope services when in doubt
  • Provide global controls.

A third matters most once an agent decides rather than suggests: make clear why the system did what it did, which drew one of the highest violation counts in the study.

A decision without an explanation leaves a person who can repeat the call but never defend it, which is why I keep an entry on Explainability at UX Guidelines.

Agents need all three, plus two things a 2019 product rarely needed:

  • The first is a record the agent didn’t write. Replit’s agent misreported its own recovery options.
  • The second is a stop that works mid-flight, on screen while the agent runs, plus an escalation path for when it wants to step past its mandate.

I’ve worked inside a lot of these loops. In legal tech at the companies I managed teams at, we always built guardrails that made lawyers review contract language before it moved. We worked just as hard on making that review easy to do, because a required step that’s painful gets rubber-stamped. Maccarone adds the other half: review holds only when the reviewer has something to lose, like a name or a license.

A rubber stamp is a loop no human truly owns.

So when does human in the loop stop meaning human owning the loop? The moment the person in it can no longer pass the reach test. That happens when approvals outpace reading, when the only fence is a sentence in a prompt, or when the only account of events is the agent’s own. Any one of those is enough to turn a reviewer into a witness.

Keep the Initiative

So, should an agent act before you ask? Often, yes; an agent that never acts first is slower. The useful version gets the work ready while you’re busy, then waits at the edge of anything it can’t take back.

Who is accountable when it does more than you authorized? Not the person who clicked approve on a summary they couldn’t check. Whoever sets the reach owns the result. What happens inside the mandate belongs to whoever granted it. Anything outside it belongs to the team that built an agent able to get there.

That’s less comfortable for builders than a confirm dialog, which is the point. A dialog lets a team ship autonomy and park the liability elsewhere. Elish’s crumple zone is what you get by default when you design around a watcher instead of for one.

Human in the loop was a good phrase for a world where software waited. Agents don’t wait, so the phrase has to carry more than a button can hold. Agency matters, and it stays useful only while the people an agent works for remain in control of it.

Build agents that pass the reach test in plain view, and the loop becomes theirs.

Make These Four Moves

  • Audit the approvals. Measure how long people spend before clicking approve; if most approvals land within seconds, you’ve built a ritual rather than a review.
  • Write the rules. List what the agent may do, on which data, and until when, then enforce it in permissions, not the prompt.
  • Run the reach test. Let the agent act unasked on anything a person can undo in one step, and require a decision for anything they can’t.
  • Keep an independent record. Log actions outside the agent’s own narration, and keep a working stop control on screen while it runs.

Human in the loop means making sure the human is not out of the loop was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: The AI experience doesn’t care about your org chart
text:
The AI experience doesn’t care about your org chart

AI is bringing content design, enterprise content strategy, knowledge management, and model behavior into the same user experience. Our ways of working haven’t caught up.

Imagine a finance manager trying to understand why a supplier hasn’t been paid.

The enterprise application shows that the invoice has been approved. The manager asks the AI assistant when the supplier can expect payment, and the assistant explains that the invoice has completed the approval process and is ready for payment.

Except it isn’t.

The invoice is blocked because of a discrepancy between the invoiced amount and the purchase order. Approval and payment eligibility are different things, governed by different parts of the business process.

The assistant hasn’t necessarily misunderstood the approval status. But it has failed to understand what that status means in relation to everything else.

Maybe it retrieved documentation about invoice approvals without the information about payment blocks. Maybe the underlying business concepts aren’t represented consistently across systems. Maybe it didn’t have access to the current payment status. Or maybe it had the right information and still failed to interpret it correctly.

Those are different problems, often owned by different teams.

But from the user’s perspective, it’s one experience — and it’s broken.

This is one of the most consequential challenges emerging as AI becomes part of enterprise software. We’re bringing together content and knowledge ecosystems that we’ve historically managed separately, and we haven’t yet developed the ways of working to manage their interdependence.

We’re going to need more than better AI models, better content systems, or better design guidelines. We’re going to need to rethink how these things work together.

We’re talking about more than one AI transformation

One thing that makes this moment difficult to navigate is that we tend to talk about AI and content as though we’re discussing a single change.

We’re not.

In a 2026 article for Nielsen Norman Group, Sarah Gibbons articulated four different meanings of “AI design”: designing with AI, designing AI products, designing for AI agents, and designing the AI itself.

That distinction is useful because the implications for content work are dramatically different depending on which kind of AI design we’re talking about.

Consider two scenarios.

In the first, a product team uses AI to accelerate its existing design process. It has a content design system with established terminology, voice and tone guidelines, and interaction patterns. Designers use AI to generate candidate UI copy, and content designers review and refine it before shipping.

AI has changed how efficiently the team produces content, but the fundamental model is familiar. People design and approve a defined set of content before it ships, and the product displays that content according to established rules and conditions.

In the second scenario, the product generates content dynamically for each user, drawing on information about their task, their context, the state of the system, and relevant enterprise knowledge.

The content designer can’t anticipate or approve every possible sentence. Instead, they help design the system that determines what the experience should communicate, under what conditions, with which constraints, and how to evaluate whether it’s working.

That’s a fundamentally different design challenge.

And then there’s another dimension: an AI agent that needs to understand the same product well enough to take action on behalf of a user. The information and structures that make sense to humans may not be sufficient for an agent. The system needs reliable representations of concepts, relationships, actions, constraints, and permissions.

Those three situations map to the first three of Gibbons’s categories. The fourth, designing the AI itself, is what is being called things like model design, model behavior, context architecutre, or content engineering — and it shapes all of the others.

These scenarios don’t replace one another. They increasingly coexist, sometimes within the same product.

We’re only beginning to understand what that means for content work.

Specialization is increasing. So is interdependence.

There’s been considerable discussion about whether content design is splitting into different specializations.

One direction moves deeper into content systems: structured content, reusable patterns, guidelines, standards, and the infrastructure that allows content design decisions to scale.

Another moves toward model behavior design: shaping how AI systems communicate, interpret intent, manage ambiguity, explain their decisions, and respond in different situations.

I see value in recognizing these areas of expertise. They involve different technical knowledge, methods, and deliverables.

But there’s another area where content designers need to develop greater expertise: the semantic and context architecture that allows systems to work with meaning.

Taxonomies, ontologies, and knowledge graphs are becoming increasingly relevant to the experiences we’re designing.

These aren’t interchangeable technologies. Taxonomies help organize and classify concepts. Ontologies define concepts and relationships within a domain. Knowledge graphs can represent interconnected information in ways that systems can query and use.

Together, these kinds of structures can help establish shared meaning across systems.

A broader context architecture also needs to account for information about the user’s task, the current state of the product, relevant business rules, permissions, and other conditions that determine what information is appropriate at a particular moment.

For content designers, learning these concepts well enough to communicate with technical teams is a start.

But content designers should also learn to actively help shape the semantic architecture of the experiences they design.

Information architects, knowledge engineers, data specialists, and enterprise architects bring essential expertise to that work. Content designers add what has always been central to our discipline: terminology, conceptual models, information organization, user mental models, and the relationship between language and understanding.

The decisions encoded in a semantic model can have direct consequences for how a user experiences a product.

If a system represents two business concepts as equivalent when users understand them as distinct, that mismatch may surface in navigation, generated explanations, recommendations, or agent behavior.

That’s a UX problem, even if its source is several layers removed from the interface.

This is also why I’m cautious about drawing hard boundaries between emerging content specializations.

We need people who go deep into content systems, model behavior, and semantic architecture. But their work needs to share patterns, concepts, and principles if the experience is going to feel coherent.

An enterprise user might move between a traditional interface, dynamically generated explanations, an AI conversation, and an agent performing a task.

Those interactions won’t use identical language or behave in identical ways, nor should they. But they need to share an understanding of how the product works.

Specialization makes sense. Separation is where I get concerned.

AI is bringing separate content ecosystems into the same experience

The challenge becomes even larger when we look beyond UX content design.

Enterprises have long divided responsibility for content and knowledge across different domains.

UX content design teams work on product experiences, language, interaction patterns, and design systems. Technical communication teams create and maintain product documentation, help content, and educational materials. Marketing, support, and other functions manage their own content ecosystems.

Content strategy and content ops establish content models, workflows, governance, lifecycle processes, and systems for managing content at scale, but usually within individual domains rather than across them.

Information architecture shapes how information is organized, labeled, and connected within each of these domains. Knowledge management varies even more: in some organizations it means maintaining documentation and knowledge bases, and in others it means capturing, sharing, and applying organizational expertise.

Now AI engineering teams are building systems that retrieve knowledge, assemble context, generate responses, and enable agents to act, often drawing on content and information governed by all these different functions.

These connections aren’t entirely new. Documentation has always needed to reflect how products actually work. Terminology in an interface should be consistent with the language in support content. But teams could often manage these dependencies through periodic reviews, handoffs, and separate publication processes.

AI is changing the nature of that dependency.

An AI assistant might draw on technical documentation to answer a question within a product. The semantic architecture can influence what information it retrieves and how it interprets that information. Content design patterns can shape how the assistant communicates its response. And business rules and permissions can determine what actions an agent can take on the user’s behalf.

The experience is increasingly assembled from information and design decisions managed by different teams, sometimes in real time.

That creates new operational challenges. When something goes wrong, no single team may have the visibility or authority to diagnose and fix the problem. And a change made in one system can have consequences for experiences that another team owns.

This is why content ops and design ops need to work much more closely together. But the coordination can’t stop there. It also needs to involve the people responsible for enterprise knowledge, semantic architecture, AI engineering, and evaluation.

We need to scale coordinated decisions

Large enterprises have always struggled to scale content design.

One response has been to invest in reusable patterns, standards, guidelines, design systems, and operational processes that allow teams to create more consistent experiences without requiring a content designer to personally review every decision.

But another response, less often acknowledged, has been to accept uneven quality. When headcount shrinks or demand exceeds capacity, some experiences simply receive less attention. That compromise was never ideal, but organizations could often contain its consequences within particular products or channels.

AI makes that compromise harder to sustain. Inconsistencies in terminology, guidance, or source content can now influence generated responses and actions across many interactions.

Investments in reusable systems are becoming even more essential. AI can also make them more powerful by bringing guidance directly into the tools and workflows where experiences are designed and built.

But scaling content production isn’t the same as scaling content design.

AI can help us generate more content, more quickly. That doesn’t guarantee the content is appropriate, coherent, accurate, or useful.

Scaling content design means making good design decisions repeatable across an organization.

And increasingly, those decisions don’t live in one team’s tools or processes.

Consider what happens when an enterprise changes the terminology for an important business concept.

Traditionally, a content design team might update the design system and work with product teams to change UI strings. A documentation team might update help content and published materials according to its own release process.

Now we may also need to consider whether the change affects a taxonomy or ontology, what an AI assistant retrieves, which terms it uses in generated explanations, how an agent interprets a request, and what our evaluation tests consider a correct response.

Who identifies all those dependencies? Who decides which changes are significant? How do the changes move through the different systems? How do we know when they’re complete?

These are operational questions.

Combining all these functions into one organization could create as many problems as it solves.

What we need is a more integrated operating model: shared standards where they matter, clear ownership, connected workflows, and governance that accounts for how decisions propagate across systems.

In practice, that means:

  • Shared governance of enterprise terminology and semantic standards, so a change to an important business concept is made deliberately and carried everywhere it matters.
  • Content design patterns that inform both traditional interfaces and AI behavior, so the product communicates as one product.
  • Workflows that identify which experiences need review when enterprise knowledge changes, so teams find the dependencies before users do.
  • Feedback loops that run in the other direction, so what we learn about AI behavior and user understanding reaches the teams who can fix the source.

That last one deserves more attention than it usually gets.

If testing reveals that an AI assistant consistently misunderstands a business concept, how does that information reach the teams responsible for the underlying knowledge, semantic structure, or content model?

If a documentation team discovers that users misunderstand a particular process, how does that insight influence the design of the product and its AI interactions?

We’ve spent years developing ways to scale the work within content functions. Now we need to get better at scaling the work across them.

Evaluation is becoming part of content and experience operations

Evaluation is another area where this interdependence becomes clear.

With traditional UI content, we can review a relatively stable set of artifacts before they ship. We can assess the language, test it with users, and make revisions.

When an AI system generates responses dynamically, we can’t review every possible output in advance.

Instead, we need to evaluate the system’s behavior across different situations and continue evaluating it as the system, its knowledge, and its users’ needs change.

We’re still at a very early stage of learning how to do this well.

Much of the initial work must be exploratory. People examine outputs, identify patterns, form hypotheses about why something went wrong, and determine what needs to change.

As with the invoice, the cause can sit in several places. Sometimes the issue is with the model’s behavior. Sometimes the system retrieved the wrong information. Sometimes the underlying content was incomplete, outdated, or contradictory. Sometimes the system lacked the context necessary to interpret the request correctly.

And sometimes the response is factually accurate but still represents a poor experience.

It might misunderstand the user’s intent, communicate uncertainty inappropriately, fail to explain an important limitation, or suggest an action without adequately establishing what the user wants.

These are different kinds of problems, and they require different kinds of expertise.

I expect we’ll get much better at translating what we learn into evals: repeatable tests that assess how AI systems perform against defined expectations. These can help us identify recurring failures, assess the impact of changes, and improve the system over time.

But first, we need to understand what we’re evaluating.

It’s not enough to ask whether a response is accurate. We also need to ask whether it was appropriate in context, supported the user’s goals, and made sense as part of the overall experience. And when the system recommends or takes action, we need to evaluate whether users understand what’s happening and retain appropriate control.

Go back to the finance manager. An evaluation that only checked whether the assistant described the approval status accurately would have passed that response. The manager still wouldn’t know when the supplier would be paid.

One tempting response to poor AI outputs is to give the system more context. But more isn’t necessarily better. Irrelevant, outdated, or conflicting information can actually make responses less reliable. The challenge is determining which knowledge, rules, and details about the user’s task are needed in a particular situation, and using evaluation to understand whether we’re providing the right context.

This is another place where content designers and strategists, design researchers, AI engineers, and the people responsible for enterprise knowledge and semantic architecture need to work closely together.

As these practices mature, we’ll be able to automate more of our evaluations. But human judgment will remain essential, not only for assessing outputs, but for identifying new failure patterns and refining our understanding of what good AI behavior looks like.

This is particularly important for experience quality, where success depends on context, user expectations, and judgments that aren’t always easily reduced to pass-or-fail criteria. Automated evals and human evaluation will need to work together, each informing and improving the other.

The operational challenge will be to turn what we learn through evaluation into improvements across the systems involved.

An evaluation finding shouldn’t stop at identifying a bad response. It should help us diagnose what needs to change, whether that’s the model’s instructions, the knowledge it retrieves, the semantic architecture, the interaction patterns, or even the underlying business process. And that diagnosis needs to reach the people who can address it.

Those changes then need to be governed, tested, and maintained.

Evaluation used to be a checkpoint at the end of the design process. It’s becoming one of the ways we maintain the experience itself.

Enterprise knowledge is becoming part of experience architecture

There’s a larger shift underneath all of this.

We’ve often treated content as something we produce, manage, and deliver through products and systems.

But AI is making content and knowledge increasingly important to what those products and systems can understand, communicate, and do.

Enterprise knowledge is becoming part of experience architecture.

That doesn’t mean every document becomes a product component, or that every content specialist needs to become an AI engineer.

It means decisions about how information is structured, represented, governed, and made available can directly shape the behavior and quality of an experience.

And it means the distinction between designing an experience and designing the knowledge that supports it is becoming harder to maintain.

I’m not suggesting that anyone has figured out the right organizational structures or operating models for this work. I certainly haven’t. We’re just beginning to understand the scope of the transformation, and the practices we need will develop through experimentation, collaboration, and learning from real systems.

But I’m increasingly convinced that improving each discipline independently won’t be enough.

We’ll need deeper expertise in content systems, model behavior, semantic architecture, and the work of creating, organizing, and maintaining enterprise knowledge. Just as importantly, we’ll need better ways of connecting the people and systems responsible for them.

Five years from now, I suspect it will seem obvious that we couldn’t design intelligent experiences while treating product content, enterprise knowledge, and AI behavior as largely separate concerns.

We’ll still need specialists. These are complex areas that deserve deep expertise.

But I think we’ll also have developed a much more integrated understanding of what we’re collectively designing.

The experience doesn’t care about our org chart.

Increasingly, our org chart has to care about the experience.

title: Nobody wants your AI app
text:
Nobody wants your AI app

The people buying AI are blunt about the fact that the future is intelligence that disappears into existing platforms. Everyone wants it invisible and under their total control at the same time.

We are all racing to build AI apps that nobody wants to open.

Specifically, the standalone AI app, the thing you download, log into, and go to, is a worse idea than almost anyone building in the space wants to admit.

The numbers are brutal. According to RevenueCat’s analysis of more than 115,000 apps, AI apps are fantastic at getting you to sign up and terrible at getting you to stay. They convert free users to paid faster than regular apps, then lose them roughly a third faster.

A year in, only about one in five subscribers is still paying.

The pattern is simple and a little embarrassing. People try the AI app, get their “wow,” and then just stop opening it, because, often, it was just a novelty experience. Venture firm Bessemer has started warning that even business AI tools are heading for the same cliff unless they get themselves embedded into something people already use every day.

This is basically the same problem people had with Google+ (remember that?). Google got hundreds of millions of people to sign up, and then 90 percent of sessions lasted under five seconds.

You can build a gorgeous destination, pour a fortune into it, and get everyone to sign up once, and it still dies if nobody comes back.

Nir Eyal called what these app are missing the Hook Model, that products become habits through a loop of trigger, action, reward, and investment, each pass making the next one more likely. A novelty AI app nails the middle of that loop, you act, you get your clever reward, once, but there’s nothing pulling you back tomorrow and nothing that costs you to simply walk away from it. The loop never closes, so a habit never forms.

On the enterprise side, the rejection is blunter and faster. I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve heard large companies insist they are not taking on yet another tool. At this point, they often already have their own internal AI product and don’t want a new destination, a new login, a new thing for their people to remember to visit.

They want the capability dropped inside the systems they already use, where the work already happens. Snyk, a security firm, studied more than 3,000 enterprise environments and found exactly that. Companies are stitching AI into their existing stack, not buying standalone products to use in parallel.

This is bigger than a retention problem.

The destination is dying. Not AI, AI is everywhere and growing. The app is dying.

The idea that you deliver intelligence by building a place for people to come get it is over. The future is no app at all, intelligence woven invisibly into the tools people already live in, surfacing when it’s useful and getting out of the way when it isn’t.

While that may sound clean, it isn’t. The same companies that want the AI invisible also want it completely under their control. They want it to disappear into the workflow and they want a dashboard, an audit trail, a record of every time it ran and what it touched.

Invisible to the user, totally visible to the owner.

Those two desires are at war, and whoever satisfies both at once is going to win the next decade of AI products.

We need to take stock of why the app model is collapsing, what the people buying AI actually want instead, why “invisible” is so much harder than it sounds, and where the real work, and the real careers, are moving.

The companies still pouring money into beautiful standalone AI apps are building tollbooths on a road people have already started to abandon.

The app everyone downloaded and nobody kept

Surprise, it’s not Quibi!

Malika Aubakirova and Anjney Midha at a16z, working with OpenRouter, analyzed more than 100 trillion tokens of real-world AI usage. Stickiness, they found, doesn’t depend on your product’s interface or features, but rather on the capabilities of the underlying model.

The same study found that fewer than one in ten weekly ChatGPT users ever bothers to try a competing assistant, despite there being zero cost to do it. People plant themselves in one big AI and stay.

They will not leave ChatGPT. They will drop your ChatGPT wrapper in a week. Stickiness lives with the model and churn lives with the destination you built on it.

People aren’t loyal to your app. They’re loyal to the intelligence inside it, and that intelligence is for rent, to everyone, including you.

This is why the AI app graveyard is filling up so fast. Character.AI lost roughly 60 percent of its user base in a year.

Jasper, one of the early AI-writing darlings, watched more than half its revenue evaporate.

Google+ had hundreds of millions of accounts and almost no one who came back. A gorgeous destination nobody had a reason to visit twice.

Yupp, an AI startup that raised thirty-three million dollars and signed up 1.3 million users, shut down anyway, with its founders explaining that the models underneath improved so fast that they never found a durable reason for anyone to keep coming back.

Over a million people used the product and it still wasn’t a business..

If that pattern feels familiar, it should. This is basically the MoviePass story with better branding (and I worked on MoviePass!).

Millions signed up overnight. There was no durable business underneath, and it collapsed in a heap. A lot of AI apps are basically following this same model.

MoviePass got millions of people to sign up almost overnight for something that felt like a cheat code, and the spectacular sign-up numbers meant nothing once it turned out there was no durable business underneath. Massive adoption, a value proposition that dissolved on contact with reality, and a collapse that happened faster than anyone expected.

A lot of today’s AI apps are doing the exact same thing.

Brian Balfour, the founder of Reforge and former head of growth at HubSpot, calls this “product-market fit collapse.” In normal software, customer expectations rise slowly, so a product that nails its market can coast for a while. In AI, he points out, expectations reset almost instantly.

Every time a new model drops, users recalibrate what “good” even means, and dropping your app for whatever is newer, or for the raw model underneath it, costs them nothing. You are not building toward a stable finish line because the finish line keeps moving away from you every few months.

We have a category with astonishing sign-up rates, near-zero switching costs, expectations that reset on a monthly basis, and no loyalty to anything except the model you don’t own.

That same body of research points, almost accidentally, at the way out. The a16z study describes what it calls a “glass slipper” effect. When a user’s actual workflow fits a particular model so precisely that it creates real inertia, a cost, finally, to leaving. The apps that retain are the ones that have wedged themselves so deeply into something a person does every day that walking away would actually hurt.

The answer is quite simple. Stop building a place for people to visit and start building something they can’t easily remove.

What the people buying AI actually want

Larger companies say they aren’t adding another AI tool the way someone declines a second helping at a dinner they’re already full from. These are organizations that have spent two years drowning in AI pilots, logins, dashboards, and Chrome extensions, and they have hit a wall.

Companies do not want another destination. They want the capability, the actual intelligence, dropped inside the systems their people already use, where the work already happens.

The most striking version of it I’ve heard is that you shouldn’t even have to know you’re using a different product. You should just know that the thing you were doing got better.

That is a remarkable thing for a company to say about a product it is paying for, and it is becoming the default expectation rather than the exception. The same instinct shows up outside the enterprise too. A news organization I talked with recently had no interest in building another app for people to download. They wanted their journalism to show up where people already are, in a text message, inside the AI assistant someone is already talking to, with no new place to go.

This is where the measurable center of gravity has already moved, and the infrastructure numbers show it.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP), the open standard that lets AI reach into the tools and data a company already uses, went from a developer curiosity to something closer to 97 million downloads a month and production use inside roughly 40 percent of technical organizations. Gartner expects that by the end of the 2026, 40 percent of enterprise applications will ship with task-specific AI agents built in.

The designers paying attention have already clocked what this does to the job. Patrick Neeman puts it bluntly, that chat was only ever an interface, and agents are something else entirely.

The design work, he argues, has moved to the contract underneath the product, the rules and handshakes that let one system quietly hand a task to another and get a trustworthy answer back. When the interface disappears, the thing you’re actually designing is the behavior.

Think about what “invisible utility” has always looked like once a technology matures. Mark Weiser, the Xerox PARC scientist who coined the term “ubiquitous computing,” put it in a line that has aged remarkably well. “The most profound technologies are those that disappear. They weave themselves into the fabric of everyday life until they are indistinguishable from it.”

Mark Weiser called it in 1991. “The most profound technologies are those that disappear.” He was describing the future of the interface before most of us had one. AI is finally proving him right.

Nobody opens an app to use electricity. You don’t launch a program to get water out of the tap. The most important technologies succeeded precisely by disappearing, by becoming something simply present in the walls, available the instant you need it and invisible the rest of the time.

That is the shape AI is racing toward, and the companies building beautiful standalone AI destinations are, in a sense, trying to sell you a generator and a trip to the well at the exact moment everyone else is wiring the building.

The holy grail is a world where one AI simply calls another. Google’s Agent-to-Agent protocol, now governed by the Linux Foundation and adopted across more than 150 organizations, exists precisely so that one company’s AI can hand a task to a specialized capability elsewhere and get a usable answer back, with no human opening a separate product to make it happen.

The interface vanishes completely into the workflow. It’s genuinely hard to build well, and the infrastructure is still young, but the direction is set. The companies that understand it are to disappear.

That sounds like a potential answer. Make the intelligence invisible, embed it in the workflow, and, BOOM, you win. The problem is that the people who want it invisible want something else at the very same time, something that pulls in the exact opposite direction, and that contradiction is where most of this is going to get stuck.

Nobody has figured out invisible, but watched

The answer seems to be to make AI invisible. Embed it, dissolve it into the workflow, let it work without anyone having to go anywhere. Simple.

Except it isn’t, and the reason is entirely stuck in humanity. The same companies that demand the AI be invisible to their employees demand that it be completely visible to them.

They want it to disappear into the workflow, and they want a dashboard showing every time it ran. They want it to act without being summoned, and they want an audit trail of everything it touched. They want it woven invisibly into the fabric of everyday life, to borrow Weiser’s phrase, and they want a kill switch they can reach in half a second, a demand that turns out to be mostly aspirational.

In a Writer’s enterprise survey, more than a third of employees said they couldn’t immediately pull the plug on a rogue AI agent even if they needed to. Invisible to the user, yet totally visible to the owner.

The same leaders who tell me they want our capability to vanish into their systems will, ten minutes later, ask how they’ll track exactly who used it, how often, and what it returned, so they can prove the ROI to their own bosses. One large company essentially wanted the product to be invisible to its workforce and fully instrumented for its executives at the same time.

A recurring, hard stop in these conversations is data. More than one major brand has told me, flatly, that they will not feed their proprietary information into an outside tool, no matter how good it is, and that any vendor has to guarantee the model underneath isn’t quietly learning from what they put in.

Invisible is fine. Ungoverned is a non-starter.

Security researchers now treat this as table stakes.

Becky Brooks describes how organizations need to be able to answer basic questions about every AI action, which tools it called, what data passed through, whether any of it was proprietary, and most of them can’t.

The data behind that fear is genuinely alarming. The Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, the most-cited study in enterprise security, found that employee use of unapproved AI tools tripled in a single year, to 45 percent of the workforce, with two-thirds of those people using personal accounts outside any corporate control.

Cyberhaven’s analysis found the average employee now feeds sensitive data into an AI tool about once every three days.

IBM’s Cost of a Data Breach report found that a growing majority of breached companies had no governance in place to manage AI or even detect its unapproved use.

The AI already has disappeared into the workflow.

It gets starker when you look at the actual network traffic. Infrastructure company Kong examined enterprise AI usage running through its systems and found that fewer than 1 percent of organizations had any AI-specific governance controls in place.

Meanwhile, almost 98 percent of their AI requests were flowing out to third-party proprietary services, every one of them carrying prompts, context, and often sensitive data outside the company’s own walls.

OutSystems found 94 percent of organizations worried that AI sprawl is piling up complexity, technical debt, and security risk, while only around 12 percent have any centralized way to manage it. Everyone feels the car accelerating. Almost nobody has their hands on the wheel.

There’s an old piece of political wisdom that fits this moment better than it has any right to. “Trust, but verify.” The companies buying AI have landed in exactly that posture, except the technology has made the two halves nearly impossible to hold at once.

The whole appeal of invisible AI is that you don’t have to watch it. The whole fear of invisible AI is that you can’t.

A thing designed to operate without your attention is, by definition, a thing operating outside your attention, and that is a terrifying property to hand a system that can touch your data, your customers, and your decisions.

This is the actual product problem of the next decade. The winning AI products will be the ones that pull off the paradox of being genuinely invisible to the person doing the work, and genuinely transparent to the person who owns the risk.

Disappear for the user. Light up like a control room for the owner. The teams that treat “invisible” as the whole goal are going to build things no serious company will deploy, because they solved for elegance and ignored accountability. The teams that bury everything in dashboards and approval gates will build something so visible and so clunky that it’s just another tool nobody opens, which puts us right back where we started.

Enterprises want the AI invisible to their people and lit up like this for themselves: every action logged, every data path visible. Invisible to the user, accountable to the owner. Almost nobody has built both.

Getting both right is brutally hard. It’s also the only version of this that actually wins.

Move Up the Stack or Get Buried in It

If you design or build products for a living, this could read like a eulogy for your job. It isn’t. The app dying is not the same as the work dying.

The work moved, and the people who notice where it went are going to be fine. The people who keep polishing the thing that’s going away are the ones who should be nervous.

Nielsen Norman Group has been studying how people actually use software since before most AI founders could type, put it about as plainly as it can be put, AI didn’t kill UX, it moved where the value lives.

The interface, the screen, the thing we used to spend all our time perfecting, is becoming a commodity. You can generate a competent one in an afternoon now. What you cannot generate in an afternoon is the judgment about what the system should do, when it should speak up, when it should stay quiet, what it’s allowed to touch, and how a human stays in control of something built to run without them.

Patrick Neeman has a sharp way of framing the trap we have to design our way out of. The reason everyone reached for chat, he argues, is that conversation is good enough at standing in for everything that it can hide the real product rather than reveal it.

The thing that feels like the answer, a text box you talk to, is often the thing keeping you from building what the moment actually needs.

The designer’s job used to be drawing the screen. Now it’s deciding the behavior, the rules and handshakes underneath, the contract between systems that no user will ever see but every user will feel.

The hardest, highest-value version of that work is the paradox from a minute ago, made real.

Mangus Eriksen lands on the exact tension this whole piece has been circling. Invisible AI only works if people trust it, and trust requires transparency and real control, without burying that control three menus deep. Read that next to the governance data from earlier and you have the entire job description for the next decade of product work.

Make it disappear for the person using it. Make it accountable to the person who owns it. Hide the machinery, surface the controls. That is a genuinely hard design problem, and it is nothing like designing a prettier chat window.

Think about what happened to the switchboard operator. In the early 20th century, connecting phone calls by hand was one of the most common jobs for young women in America. Then AT&T automated it, and the economists James Feigenbaum and Daniel Gross documented what followed. Once a city switched to dial, the operator jobs didn’t shrink, they vanished, dropping 50 to 80 percent and never coming back.

The need underneath, connecting people reliably, didn’t vanish at all. It moved up the stack, into switching systems and the engineers who design them, and it got more valuable. The part that matters is this: the women who were operators mostly didn’t make that jump.

The function moved up, and a lot of the people defined by the old version of it got left behind. The ones who thrived were the ones who moved to the layer underneath before they were forced to.

This connects to something that’s becoming ubiquitous in AI. Nobody is coming to hand you the next version of your job. Not in the broad economy, and not in our corner of it.

The people who make it through every one of these shifts are the ones who stop defending the thing they were good at and start building the thing the new world actually needs, before they’re forced to. In this case, that means letting go of the beautiful destination and getting good at the invisible, accountable system underneath it.

The future of AI is the intelligence woven so completely into the tools people already use that they stop noticing it’s there, with a clean pane of glass that lets whoever is responsible see exactly what it’s doing. Invisible to the user. Accountable to the owner. Almost nobody is building for both yet, which is precisely why it’s the opportunity.

The companies still pouring money into gorgeous standalone AI apps are building elegant tollbooths on a road people have already started to leave. The winners are somewhere else entirely, down in the plumbing, making the intelligence disappear into the work and handing the owner the keys to watch it.

The destination is dead. The infrastructure is where everything now lives.

References and further reading

Why the app model is collapsing

Malika Aubakirova, Anjney Midha, Alex Atallah, Chris Clark, Justin Summerville, State of AI: An Empirical 100 Trillion Token Study. Stickiness depends on the underlying model, not your interface; fewer than 10% of users switch despite zero cost.

RevenueCat, 2026 State of Subscription Apps Report. AI apps churn 30 to 36 percent faster than non-AI apps; only about 1 in 5 subscribers remains after a year.

Bessemer Venture Partners, Seven Product Strategies to Prevent Churn for B2B AI App Leaders. Even B2B AI tools face the churn cliff unless embedded in a daily workflow.

Brian Balfour (Reforge), on product-market fit collapse. In AI, customer expectations reset almost instantly and switching is trivial.

Google+ (Wikipedia). The destination that signed up hundreds of millions and became a ghost town, with 90 percent of sessions under five seconds.

MoviePass (Wikipedia). Spectacular sign-ups, no durable business underneath, fast collapse.

What the buyers actually want

Snyk, State of Agentic AI Adoption. Across 3,000-plus enterprise environments, organizations are embedding AI into their existing stack rather than buying standalone tools; the real AI footprint is roughly 3x the model list.

The Enterprise MCP Guide. The Model Context Protocol’s near-vertical adoption, roughly 97 million monthly downloads and production use in about 40 percent of technical organizations.

Gartner, via OutSystems research. 40 percent of enterprise applications will ship with task-specific AI agents by the end of the year.

Patrick Neeman, Headless AI Will Make Every Product a Platform. The design work has moved to the contract underneath the product.

Mark Weiser (Wikipedia). The father of ubiquitous computing: “The most profound technologies are those that disappear.”

Google’s Agent-to-Agent protocol (via FifthRow). The Linux Foundation standard that lets one AI hand a task to another, adopted across 150-plus organizations.

Invisible, but watched

Writer, 2026 Enterprise AI Adoption Report. A third of employees say they couldn’t immediately pull the plug on a rogue AI agent.

The MCP and AI Governance Gap (Techstrong). Enterprises need to answer basic questions about every AI action, and most can’t.

Verizon, 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report. Employee use of unapproved AI tools tripled in a year to 45 percent of the workforce, two-thirds via personal accounts.

Cyberhaven, shadow AI analysis. The average employee feeds sensitive data into an AI tool about once every three days.

IBM, Cost of a Data Breach Report. A growing majority of breached companies had no governance to manage or detect AI use.

Kong, enterprise AI governance research. Fewer than 1 percent of organizations have AI-specific governance controls; almost 98 percent of AI requests go to third-party services.

OutSystems, State of AI Development. 94 percent worry about AI sprawl; only about 12 percent have centralized management.

Where the work goes

Nielsen Norman Group, on AI-native UX. AI didn’t kill UX, it moved where the value lives; the interface is becoming a commodity.

Patrick Neeman, Designing for AI Means Designing Like It’s 1999. Conversation is good enough at standing in for everything that it can hide the real product.

UXmatters, The Era of the Invisible User Interface. Invisible AI works only if people trust it, which requires transparency and real control.

James Feigenbaum and Daniel Gross, Answering the Call of Automation (Quarterly Journal of Economics). When switchboards automated, the job vanished and the incumbents mostly did not move up with the work.
